intro-statistics: Statistics answers questions about a population, the whole group of interest, using data from a sample, the part you actually measure. Answers vary, so a sample result is an estimate. It is useful only when the sample represents the population, and every result is stated in context.
variables: Observational units are the individuals in a data set, and variables are the characteristics recorded for each. Categorical variables sort units into groups; quantitative ones record amounts, discrete or continuous. A parameter describes a population, a statistic describes a sample, and a distribution tells what values a variable takes and how often.
math-fractions-percents: A part of a whole is the part divided by the whole, a decimal from 0 to 1, and a percent is that decimal times 100. Pick the whole from the words of the question, and compare groups of different sizes with decimals or percents, never raw counts.
one-categorical-tables: A frequency table counts each category; a relative frequency divides each count by the total, so relative frequencies are between 0 and 1, add to 1, and compare groups of different sizes. In a sample, the relative frequency of a category is the sample proportion p-hat , a statistic that estimates the population proportion p .
one-categorical-displays: Bar charts and pie charts display one categorical variable. A bar’s height is its count or relative frequency measured from 0; a pie’s slices are parts of one whole, so every individual must be in exactly one category. Compare groups of different sizes with relative frequencies, and check axes before trusting a picture.
one-quantitative-displays: Dotplots and stemplots show every value of a small quantitative data set; histograms group values into equal bins and show the count in each, and their look depends on the bin width. A cumulative relative frequency graph shows the proportion of values at or below each point, so a proportion between two values is a difference of heights.
describing-distributions: To describe a quantitative distribution, give its shape (symmetric, skewed toward the tail, unimodal, bimodal or uniform), its center and spread with numbers, and any unusual features such as outliers, gaps and clusters. Every description names the variable and its units, so it is in context.
math-formulas: Evaluate a formula by substituting values, then following the order of operations: grouped terms first (brackets, fraction bars, roots), then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. ∑ adds a list of terms, and a square root covers everything under it, so type brackets on a calculator.
summary-statistics: The mean and standard deviation use every value, so outliers and skew pull them; the median and IQR are resistant. Quartiles are the medians of the two halves, and the 1.5×IQR fences or the 2 standard deviation rule flag outliers. Adding a constant shifts center but not spread; multiplying by a constant scales both.
boxplots: A boxplot pictures the five-number summary: a box from Q_1 to Q_3 split at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values inside the 1.5×IQR fences, and outliers marked separately. It shows center, the spread of the middle half and skew, and about a quarter of the data lies in each section, but it hides peaks and gaps.
comparing-distributions: To compare distributions, describe each feature (shape, center, spread, outliers) with a comparing word and numbers, in context. To compare single values from different distributions, use relative position: the z-score z = (x − x-bar)/s counts standard deviations from the mean, and a percentile gives the percent of values at or below.
investigative-questions: An investigative question names the population, the variable, the parameter and the kind of conclusion wanted. A census measures everyone; sample surveys and observational studies record variables without imposing anything, so they show relationships but confounding blocks cause. Only an experiment, with conditions decided by chance, supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.
random-sampling: Random sampling uses chance to choose individuals from a sampling frame. A simple random sample gives every group of n the same chance; a stratified sample takes an SRS within each stratum of similar individuals; a cluster sample takes whole groups chosen at random; a systematic sample takes every kth individual after a random start. Write procedures as label, generate, skip repeats, select.
sampling-problems: Bias is a systematic error in a sampling method. Voluntary response and convenience samples are biased because they are not random; undercoverage, nonresponse and response bias can affect even random samples. To explain a bias, name it, say how the sample differs from the population and in which direction, and remember that a bigger sample does not cure it.
experimental-design: An experiment imposes treatments on experimental units and measures a response. Good designs compare treatments (often with a control or placebo), assign them at random, replicate, control other variables and blind where possible. Completely randomized, randomized block and matched pairs designs differ in how units are grouped before randomizing. Random assignment allows cause and effect; random sampling allows generalizing.
two-categorical-displays: A two-way table counts two categorical variables together. To compare groups, turn each group's counts into percents and show them as segmented or side-by-side bars, or a mosaic plot. If the percents differ between groups, the variables are associated; association in a survey does not show cause.
two-categorical-summaries: From one two-way table you can find three kinds of share. Joint: a cell over the grand total. Marginal: a row or column total over the grand total. Conditional: a cell over the total of its group. Compare groups with conditional relative frequencies; if they differ, the variables are associated.
simulation: To estimate a probability by simulation, model the chance process with a device that has the right chances, define one trial and what to record, repeat many trials, and use the share of trials with the result. More trials give a steadier estimate (the law of large numbers). A rare simulated result casts doubt on the claim behind the model.
math-inequality-words: Translate words into inequalities before computing: at least is ≥ , at most and no more than are ≤ , more than is > , fewer than is < . For counts, change strict inequalities to include the next whole number ( X < 3 is X ≤ 2 ), and list the included values to check.
probability-intro: List the sample space. If its outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is its number of outcomes over the total. Probabilities run from 0 to 1 and the outcomes' probabilities add to 1. The complement rule, P(A^c) = 1 − P(A) , is often the fastest route, especially for "at least one".
mutually-exclusive: The joint probability P(A∩B) is the chance both events happen; in a table it is one cell over the grand total. Events are mutually exclusive when that joint probability is 0. Only then can you find P(A or B) by adding P(A) and P(B).
conditional-probability: Given B, the outcomes in B are the new whole, so P(A|B) = (P(A∩B))/(P(B)) . Rearranged, the multiplication rule P(A∩B) = P(A)⋅P(B|A) is what a tree diagram does along each path. Adding paths gives a total probability, and dividing reverses a condition, which usually changes the answer.
independence-unions: Events are independent when P(A|B) = P(A) ; then the probability of both is the product P(A)⋅P(B) . Check independence with the numbers, never by assumption alone. The probability of A or B is P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) , subtracting the overlap that would be counted twice; for mutually exclusive events the overlap is 0.
random-variables: A random variable is a number from a chance process, defined in context. Its probability distribution lists each value with its probability; the probabilities are from 0 to 1 and add to 1. Probabilities of events like "at least 3" or "fewer than 3" come from adding the right values, and cumulative probabilities add everything up to a boundary.
random-variable-parameters: The mean of a discrete random variable weights each value by its probability: μ_X = ∑ x_ip_i . It is the average over many repetitions. The standard deviation σ_X = √(∑ (x_i − μ_X)²p_i) is a typical distance from that mean. Write the expression with the numbers substituted, then interpret both in context.
math-counting: A factorial n! multiplies n by each whole number below it and counts the orders of n items ( 0! = 1 ). A combination _nC_k = (n!)/(k! (n − k)!) counts the ways to choose k of n when order does not matter; it equals _nC_(n − k) .
binomial-distribution: When a yes-or-no trial repeats n times independently with the same success probability p, the number of successes is binomial: P(X = k) = (nCk)p^k(1 − p)^(n − k) , with mean np and standard deviation √(np(1 − p)) . Name the distribution and its parameters, translate the event into an inequality, and use the complement for "at least" questions. A tiny probability under a claim casts doubt on the claim.
normal-distribution: A density curve models a distribution with areas as probabilities. Normal distributions N(μ, σ) are symmetric and bell-shaped, with about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values within 1, 2 and 3 SDs. Standardize with z = (x − μ)/(σ) to find areas, or work back from an area to a boundary with x = μ + zσ . Always name the distribution, parameters, boundary and direction.
sampling-distributions: A statistic varies from sample to sample, and its sampling distribution describes how. For the sample mean, the center is μ and the spread is (σ)/(√n) , so larger samples give less variable means. By the Central Limit Theorem, for large n the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal even from a skewed population, which lets you judge whether a sample mean is surprising.
estimators: A statistic used to estimate a parameter is an estimator, and its value from one sample is a point estimate. Judge an estimator by its sampling distribution: it is unbiased when that distribution is centered at the parameter, and it has low variability when the distribution is narrow. Random selection removes bias; larger random samples reduce variability. Neither fixes the other.
sampling-dist-proportion: For random samples, p-hat is centered at p with a spread that shrinks as n grows. It has mean p and standard deviation √(p(1 − p)/n) (accurate when the sample is at most 10% of the population) and is approximately normal when np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10 . Then z = (p-hat − p)/(σ_(p-hat)) turns a question about a sample proportion into a normal probability, which you can tie back to a claim about p .
ci-one-proportion: A confidence interval for p is p-hat ± z*√(p-hat(1 − p-hat)/n) : the point estimate plus or minus a margin of error. Check random, 10% and large counts (sample successes and failures at least 10) in words first. Larger samples shrink the margin of error; higher confidence levels stretch it.
ci-one-proportion-claims: Interpret an interval with its level, its ends and the parameter in context; interpret the level as the long-run capture rate of the method. Values inside the interval are plausible. An interval gives convincing evidence for a claim like "greater than 0.60" only when every value in it is greater than 0.60; a claimed value inside the interval is plausible, which is not the same as proven.
test-one-proportion-setup: Set up a test before looking at the data. Write hypotheses about p ( H_0:p = p_0 and a one-sided or two-sided H_a chosen from the question), p defined in context, a significance level α , the procedure named (one-sample z test for a proportion), and the conditions checked in words, with large counts using p_0 .
p-values: A p-value measures how surprising the data are if H_0 is true. Assuming H_0 is true, standardize the sample proportion with z = (p-hat − p_0)/(√(p_0(1 − p_0)/n)) and find the tail area in the direction of H_a (both tails for ≠ ). That area is the p-value: the chance of a result at least as extreme as the one observed if H_0 is true. Small p-values are evidence against H_0 ; they are never the probability that H_0 is true.
test-one-proportion: A complete test runs state, plan, do, conclude. It states hypotheses about p with α , names the one-sample z test for a proportion and checks random, 10% and large counts with p_0 , computes z and the p-value, then concludes: compare the p-value with α , reject or fail to reject H_0 , and say whether there is convincing evidence for H_a about the true proportion of all ..., in context. Never accept H_0 , and claim cause only from a randomized experiment.
errors-and-power: A Type I error rejects a true H_0 (probability α ); a Type II error fails to reject a false H_0 (probability β , against a specific alternative). Describe each with the condition first and its consequence in context. Power = 1 − β is the chance of detecting a real effect; it grows with the sample size, with α , and with the distance between the true value and p_0 .
sampling-dist-two-proportions: For two independent random samples, p-hat_1 − p-hat_2 is centered at p_1 − p_2 and has standard deviation √((p_1(1 − p_1))/(n_1) + (p_2(1 − p_2))/(n_2)) : the variances add. When all four large counts are at least 10, its distribution is approximately normal, so you can find probabilities with z-scores.
ci-two-proportions: To estimate p_1 − p_2 , use the two-sample z interval (p-hat_1 − p-hat_2) ±z*√((p-hat_1(1 − p-hat_1))/(n_1) + (p-hat_2(1 − p-hat_2))/(n_2)) after checking random, 10% and large counts for each sample. Interpret it as capturing the true difference in proportions, in context and with the order of subtraction named.
ci-two-proportions-claims: To judge a claim with an interval for p_1 − p_2 , look at where 0, or the claimed value, sits. Entirely above or below 0 gives convincing evidence of a difference in that direction; an interval that contains 0 gives no convincing evidence of a difference, which is not proof of equality. State the reason, the evidence and the parameter in context.
test-two-proportions-setup: A two-sample z test for p_1 − p_2 starts from H_0:p_1 − p_2 = 0 and an alternative chosen from the question. Because the test assumes H_0 , it pools the samples, p_c = (x_1 + x_2)/(n_1 + n_2) , and checks large counts with p_c , along with two independent random samples (or random assignment) and the 10% condition.
test-two-proportions: A two-sample z test standardizes the observed difference with the pooled standard error, z = (p-hat_1 − p-hat_2)/(√(p_c(1 − p_c)(1/(n_1) + 1/(n_2)))) , finds the p-value in the direction of H_a , compares it with α , and concludes about the true proportions in context, never accepting H_0 .
chi-square-setup: A chi-square test compares a two-way table of observed counts with the counts expected if H_0 were true. Choose independence (one sample, two variables) or homogeneity (several samples or groups, one variable), state H_0 and H_a in context, find each expected count as row total times column total over the grand total, and check random, 10% and expected counts at least 5.
chi-square-test: Carrying out a chi-square test: find each expected count, add the components ((O − E)²)/E to get χ² , use the chi-square distribution with (r − 1)(c − 1) degrees of freedom for the right-tail p-value, compare it with α , and conclude about the association or the distributions in context. The largest components show where the association lies.
sampling-dist-mean: The sample mean x-bar has a sampling distribution centered at μ with standard deviation (σ)/(√n) (10% condition). It is normal for a normal population and approximately normal for n ≥ 30 by the central limit theorem. Standardize with z = (x-bar − μ)/(σ/√n) to find probabilities about a sample mean.
ci-one-mean: When σ is unknown, a confidence interval for a mean is x-bar ± t*s/(√n) with t* from the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. Check random, 10% and normal/large sample. For paired data, compute the differences and build the same interval for the mean difference μ_d .
ci-one-mean-claims: Use a t interval to judge a claim about a mean: a claimed value outside the interval is not plausible, so the interval gives convincing evidence against it; a value inside is plausible, and nothing is proven. Write it with "Because every value in the interval ..." and name the parameter in context. Interval width grows with confidence and with s , and shrinks like 1/(√n) .
test-one-mean-setup: To set up a t test for a mean, name the parameter in context, write H_0:μ = μ_0 and an alternative whose direction comes from the question, and check random, 10% and normal/large sample. For paired data, test the mean difference μ_d with a paired t test on the differences, saying which way you subtracted.
test-one-mean: Carry out a one-sample (or paired) t test by computing t = (x-bar − μ_0)/(s/√n) with n − 1 df, finding the p-value in the direction of H_a , and comparing it with α . Conclude in context with evidence language about the true mean, and interpret the p-value as a probability computed assuming H_0 .
sampling-dist-two-means: For independent random samples (or randomly assigned groups), x-bar_1 − x-bar_2 has mean μ_1 − μ_2 and standard deviation √((σ_1²)/(n_1) + (σ_2²)/(n_2)) , and it is approximately normal when each sample mean is. Use z = ((x-bar_1 − x-bar_2) − (μ_1 − μ_2))/(σ_(x-bar_1 − x-bar_2)) for probabilities.
ci-two-means: To estimate μ_1 − μ_2 from two independent samples or randomized groups, use (x-bar_1 − x-bar_2) ±t*√((s_1²)/(n_1) + (s_2²)/(n_2)) with technology df or the conservative df. Check random, 10% and normal/large sample for each group, and interpret the interval as capturing the true difference in means, in the stated order.
ci-two-means-claims: Use an interval for μ_1 − μ_2 to judge claims: if 0 is outside, there is convincing evidence of a difference in the direction of the interval's sign; if 0 is inside, there is not, and no difference is proven. Then judge practical significance by comparing the plausible values with what matters in context, and judge cause and generalization from the design.
test-two-means-setup: To set up a test for two means, decide from the design whether the data are paired or two independent groups. For two groups, define μ_1 and μ_2 in context, write H_0:μ_1 − μ_2 = 0 with an alternative from the question, and check random, 10% and normal/large sample for each group. This is a two-sample t test.
test-two-means: A two-sample t test computes t = (x-bar_1 − x-bar_2)/(√(s_1²/n_1 + s_2²/n_2)) , finds the p-value from the t distribution with technology or conservative df in the direction of H_a , and concludes about μ_1 − μ_2 in context. Random assignment allows a causal conclusion; random samples allow generalizing.
math-lines: A line y = a + bx has slope b , the change in y for each one-unit increase in x (rise over run), and y-intercept a , the value of y when x = 0 . Interpret both in context with units, and the intercept only when x = 0 makes sense.
scatterplots: A scatterplot plots two quantitative variables, explanatory on the horizontal axis and response on the vertical. Describe what you see with four features in context: direction, form, strength and unusual features such as outliers. A pattern in observational data shows association, not cause.
correlation: The correlation r = 1/(n − 1) ∑ z_xz_y gives the direction (sign) and strength (closeness to ±1 ) of a linear association. It has no units, ignores which variable is explanatory, is pulled by outliers, misses curved patterns, and says nothing about cause.
linear-models: A regression line y-hat = a + bx predicts the response from the explanatory variable. Interpret the slope as the predicted change in y for each one-unit increase in x , and the intercept as the predicted y at x = 0 when that makes sense, always in context and with "predicted". Do not extrapolate beyond the data.
residuals: A residual is actual minus predicted, y − y-hat : positive when the point is above the line, negative when below, in the units of y . A residual plot shows the residuals against x ; random scatter around 0 means a line is appropriate, while a curve or a fan shows what the line misses.
least-squares-regression: The least-squares regression line makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible; its slope is b = r(s_y)/(s_x) and it passes through (x-bar, y-bar) . Report r² , the share of the variation in y the line accounts for, and s , the typical prediction error in the units of y . Check for high-leverage and influential points, which can change the line a lot.
